articles.title_orig: Discord is ditching Electron and its new app uses less RAM
articles.title_zh: Discord is ditching Electron and its new app uses less RAM
articles.content_orig:
Discord is moving its apps fully over to the Rust programming language.
Discord is moving its apps fully over to the Rust programming language.
Discord is finally giving up on Electron, the cross-platform framework that lets developers build desktop apps using web technologies. Electron web apps are notoriously heavy on system resources, and Discord is now moving its desktop app fully to Rust — a modern programming language designed for speed and memory safety.
“We’ve been early adopters of Rust since 2018 and a lot of our infra, voice tech, and even some of the current client is already Rust, the holy grail was getting the whole client there,” explains Discord chief technology officer Stanislav Vishnevskiy in a post on X . “That means Electron goes away, and so does React Native, mobile keeps native UI but shares app code with desktop via Rust.”
Vishnevskiy also shared an image of the Discord Windows client using just 290MB of RAM, which is a clear improvement as you only have to participate in a few servers and RAM usage can easily hit 1GB or more using the current Windows app.
It’s not clear when Discord will make the full switch over to Rust, but Vishnevskiy says the company “hope to get it into testing with users soon.”

articles.title_orig: China threatens retaliation as EU mulls trade “kill-switch”
articles.title_zh: China threatens retaliation as EU mulls trade “kill-switch”
articles.content_orig:
China’s ambassador to the EU, Cai Run, threatened on Thursday to retaliate if the EU adopted unilateral measures against Chinese interests.
The statement came as the European Commission is working on a new trade defence tool, dubbed a “kill-switch,” that could cut off Chinese access to the EU market in the event of serious market disruption caused by its aggressive trade policies.
“China opposes politicising economic and trade issues, overstretching the concept of security, and resorting to unilateral or maximum pressure,” Cai said.
He added: “If the EU side insists on adopting restrictive and discriminatory measures against China, China will have to take countermeasures to firmly safeguard its interests.”
As the EU faces a record-high trade deficit with China of €1 billion a day, Brussels is seeking to protect its market from low-cost Chinese imports, which have surged by 25% over the past year, according to Chinese customs.
Last October, EU leaders tasked the European Commission with developing an instrument that could be rapidly deployed against countries whose political or economic actions have serious repercussions for the EU market.
EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič told MEPs on Wednesday that the tool should be presented by the end of the year and would allow the EU “to react much faster, even by limiting the exports into the European Union.” He added that it would target “countries which are treating us [the EU] unfairly or which are harming European interests.”
Presented as country-agnostic, the tool would nevertheless directly target Chinese interests, which rely heavily on the EU’s 450 million consumers to sell their excess of production.
France and Germany pushed for such an instrument in early October, as every EU member state now faces a trade deficit with Beijing, with Chinese imports threatening entire sectors of their industries.
The Franco-German move came amid ongoing negotiations between Brussels and Beijing, which had begun the previous June with the aim of rebalancing trade relations. It also came just days before the Commission reached a deal on 9 October to reduce Chinese imports of hybrid cars into the EU.
Since the deal on cars, talks have resumed at a technical level between EU and Chinese officials, with Brussels hoping to replicate such an agreement in other sectors. A new meeting between Šefčovič and China’s Commerce Minister Wang Wentao is scheduled for March 2027.
Given the urgency of the situation, EU leaders have also asked the Commission to adopt measures, including quotas and tariffs, against Chinese imports in the chemicals and machinery industries, as pressure on the EU market has become unsustainable for European producers.
Šefčovič has repeatedly said that, with thousands of jobs at stake in the EU, the EU-China trade issue had become a political one in Europe, with high expectations among EU citizens.
Despite ongoing talks with China since June, the Commission has continued to impose additional duties on Chinese imports entering the EU following investigations product by product that found Chinese producers were benefiting from unfair pricing or subsidies from China.
This is not the first time China has threatened the EU with countermeasures. It already did so against a bill – the Industrial Accelerator Act - currently under discussion by the EU’s co-legislators seeking to limit access to EU public procurement and impose strict conditions on investments in the EU market, also targeting Beijing without explicitly naming it.

articles.title_orig: CVS announces major breakup, pharmacy expert weighs impact on consumers
articles.title_zh: CVS announces major breakup, pharmacy expert weighs impact on consumers
articles.content_orig:
In an interview with Fox News Digital, Douglas Hoey of the National Community Pharmacists Association said splitting CVS Pharmacy from its insurance and Pharmacy Benefits Manager businesses could improve competition and lower costs.
CVS Health on Wednesday announced plans to split its sprawling conglomerate into separate health insurance and pharmacy businesses, a move one industry expert welcomed as a potential way to drive down costs for millions of Americans.
The separation is expected to be completed by the first half of 2028, creating two independent, publicly traded companies.
The healthcare solutions company, which will temporarily retain the CVS Health name, will include its pharmacy benefit manager (PBM) insurance plans and subsidiaries, including Aetna, CVS Caremark, CVS Specialty, Oak Street Health and Signify Health.
CVS Pharmacy, the company's retail division, will include roughly 9,000 stores, its mail-order pharmacy business, MinuteClinic and the Health100 technology services unit.
CVS PHARMACY REACHES $315M SETTLEMENT WITH JUSTICE DEPARTMENT OVER CONTROLLED SUBSTANCE PRESCRIPTIONS
CVS Pharmacy, the company's retail division, will include roughly 9,000 stores. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images, File / Getty Images)
Existing CVS Health investors will receive shares in both companies tax-free, according to the Woonsocket, Rhode Island-based company.
The announcement rattled investors, sending CVS shares plunging nearly 13% Wednesday to levels not seen since spring.
For independent pharmacies, however, the breakup could create a more level playing field against the retail pharmacy giant.
An industry expert representing thousands of independent pharmacies told FOX Business that the move could restore market competition, improve patient access to medications and potentially lower prescription drug costs if "CVS becomes a true partner with other pharmacies."
"We think it will be good for competition, good for patients, lower prices, good for small businesses to be able to compete against these conglomerates," Douglas Hoey of the National Community Pharmacists Association (NCPA) said.
CVS OFFERS NEW PHARMACY OPTION FOR PET OWNERS
A customer stands at the drop-off counter inside a CVS Pharmacy store. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images, File / Getty Images)
As a standalone entity, the CVS retail pharmacy business could see more store closures, Hoey added, pointing to the company's track record of shuttering roughly 10% of its locations over the past five years due to underperformance.
"With the company split off to be a CVS Pharmacy, my guess would be that they're going to look even more closely at underperforming stores and want to close underperforming stores," Hoey said. "The good news for patients is that most of the time.
"CVSs are located near other pharmacies … And so when one closes, there's usually another option, whether it's an independent or another chain that patients can choose from."
Hoey added that the separation could help level the playing field in the pharmacy market, arguing that CVS's competitive practices have contributed to the closure of independent pharmacies. Today, he said, only about one-third of pharmacies nationwide are independently owned.
FTC TO INVESTIGATE CVS CAREMARK, HUMANA, OTHER PHARMACY BENEFIT MANAGERS
A CVS MinuteClinic patient exam room in South Portland, Me. (Gabe Souza/Portland Press Herald via Getty Images, File / Getty Images)
"Independent pharmacies have gone out of business. Rite Aid has declared bankruptcy. Walgreens is no longer a publicly traded company. They were taken off the stock market because they were purchased by private equity," Hoey said.
"CVS is not only a competitor, but they decide how much their competition gets paid. They can also decide where patients can go to get their medicine ," Hoey said.
Splitting the company would mean that CVS would not be deciding "who's the judge, the jury and the executioner for all the other pharmacies?" Hoey said.
CVS may have pursued the separation for two primary reasons, Hoey said.
The move could unlock shareholder value by separating its slower-growing, lower-margin retail drugstore business from its faster-growing, more profitable healthcare divisions .
In a statement released Tuesday, CVS said the restructuring would allow the company to "evolve into two companies with greater focus and more value for stakeholders."
A CVS pharmacist prepares vaccinations at a store in Huntington Park, Calif. (Christina House / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images, File / Getty Images)
Hoey added that the split could also help the company get ahead of mounting regulatory scrutiny over vertical integration, which allows companies to steer patients, dictate drug coverage, and underpay competing pharmacies.
In 2025 and 2026, Arkansas and Tennessee, for example, passed laws barring PBMs from owning retail pharmacies, citing potential conflicts of interest. Both measures, however, are facing ongoing federal legal challenges.
"CVS decides how much other pharmacies get paid. They also decide where patients can go to get their prescriptions," Hoey said.
"In some instances, they pay themselves more than they pay other pharmacies."
However, in its legal challenge to Tennessee's law, CVS argued that PBMs operating in the state already comply with existing requirements that they "reimburse nonaffiliated pharmacies at the same or higher rate than affiliated pharmacies, and it prohibits PBMs from steering patients to affiliated pharmacies rather than nonaffiliated pharmacies."
As a standalone entity, the CVS retail pharmacy business could see more store closures, Hoey says. ( Paul Weaver/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images, File / Getty Images)
The NCPA added that while the split is a positive development, investors will continue to hold stocks in both companies, potentially giving shareholders an incentive to see the two businesses favor one another.
"We need more information as to how they're going to be regulated," Hoey said.
Additionally, CVS Specialty will remain under the company's healthcare solutions division rather than its pharmacy business.
Hoey said that means its highly lucrative specialty mail-order operations, which handle high-cost medications for cancer, multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis, as well as GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic, will remain part of the PBM and insurance business.
CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO
As a result, potential conflicts of interest involving patient steering and drug rebate arrangements could remain a concern in the specialty medication market.
"They should behave like a regular pharmacy, but we'll see how that goes. We need more information as to how they're going to be regulated," Hoey said.
CVS did not immediately respond to FOX Business' request for comment.

articles.title_orig: The midterms could fuel the K-shaped AI trade
articles.title_zh: The midterms could fuel the K-shaped AI trade
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. midterms could widen the AI divide: tighter data center rules may reward tech giants with capacity in hand and squeeze debt-funded companies trying to catch up.
Democratic victories in key gubernatorial races raised the prospect of tougher scrutiny for data center projects, adding to investor concerns about how quickly new capacity can be built and financed.
In Texas, Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has proposed a statewide moratorium on new data center permits, although projects already under construction would reportedly be exempt.
As the markets digested the results on Wednesday, Microsoft and Amazon each surged more than 6%, while AI infrastructure provider CoreWeave plunged around 10%. Chipmakers Micron and Nvidia fell 7% and 3.17%, respectively.
Differences in borrowing costs are playing a key role in the split, James Sullivan, managing director and co-head of global fundamental research at JPMorgan, told CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia " on Thursday.
Sullivan said borrowing spreads have widened significantly for neocloud companies, leaving their cost of additional capital substantially higher than that of hyperscalers that benefit from more diversified customers and revenue streams.
"The fact that you're seeing this bifurcation in equity performance is largely driven by the view that existing capacity is significantly more valuable now because of incremental supply constraints," he said.
The midterm results could reinforce that view if they make new projects more vulnerable to permitting delays.
BMI warned that a sharp slowdown in data center construction and AI investment could produce a greater-than-expected decline in overall investment, The Business Times reported, citing the firm's post-midterm analysis.
The potential impact is uneven across the construction pipeline. Much of the data center capacity expected to come online in 2027 is already under construction, limiting the near-term impact of new restrictions.
Projects planned for 2028 face greater exposure to permitting delays and regulatory uncertainty, investment bank Nomura said in a note Wednesday about the midterm results.
Tighter regulations on data center construction could become a more significant headwind to AI investment from 2028, the firm said.
Shares of Nvidia-backed neocloud CoreWeave, Nebius and Iren fell at least 30% in October, as tightening credit markets raised questions about how AI infrastructure projects would be financed . CoreWeave's five-year credit default swap spread has surged past 1,100 basis points, reflecting rising costs for investors seeking protection against a potential default.
The distinction may be how well companies can absorb delays and fund the capacity they do build. Hyperscalers have broader cloud businesses and more internally generated cash flow, while lower-rated neoclouds face greater exposure to borrowing costs, energy prices and refinancing conditions, JPMorgan Asset Management said in an Oct. 20 research note.
The asset manager said financially stronger hyperscalers could also secure cheaper capacity or acquire assets if weaker operators scale back.

articles.title_orig: Trump's Fed pressure campaign hits a new Democratic wall in the Senate
articles.title_zh: Trump's Fed pressure campaign hits a new Democratic wall in the Senate
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Democrats secured control of the Senate on Tuesday, a seismic shift that effectively blocks President Trump's campaign to reshape the Federal Reserve and neutralizes what many analysts viewed as a threat to the central bank's independence.
It also heightens the challenge for Trump should he maneuver to replace any sitting officials.
"Democrats' control of the Senate reclaims the party's ability to approve or deny the President's nominees for judges and heads of other executive branch agencies," Jonathan Pingle, an economist for UBS, wrote in a note. "That includes the need for Democrats to approve any new members of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System should one of the existing governors step aside."
That political firewall directly impacts the administration's ongoing effort to remove Fed governor Lisa Cook. Trump fired Cook in August 2025, claiming she committed mortgage fraud by making misrepresentations on loan documents years before her appointment to the central bank. Cook, a Biden appointee, has denied any wrongdoing and sued. The lawsuit has gone through multiple court rungs before reaching the Supreme Court earlier this year.
Last month, Trump established a committee to determine whether her statements constituted legal "cause" for removal from the central bank, signaling that his efforts to oust her are continuing.
Read more: How much control does the president have over the Fed and interest rates?
However, Tuesday's election significantly changed the stakes of that investigation. Michael Feroli, chief US economist for JPMorgan, noted that the Senate flip alters the math for the White House.
"Even a successful removal would not open a seat up to a friend of the administration," Feroli wrote in a client note.
Jaret Seiberg, analyst with TD Cowen, agreed that the inability to confirm a replacement may make Trump less inclined to fire Cook.
Not everyone is convinced the administration will back down, however. Loretta Mester, former head of the Cleveland Fed, told Yahoo Finance, "Perhaps it makes it less likely he will succeed, but I'm not convinced it will stop the president from trying."
More broadly, Democrats taking power in Congress changes the atmosphere in which Fed officials work to set monetary policy devoid of political influence.
Trump has been vocal and persistent in urging policymakers to lower interest rates. The central bank has held steady, raising rates at times despite the White House pressure. The new power dynamic gives them more cover.
"The election result means the president has less leverage — on Congress, on the country and on the Fed," Daleep Singh, chief global economist at PGIM and a former senior official in the Biden administration, said in an interview on Bloomberg Television. "Voters are angry about the rising cost of living. You put those two thoughts together, and the Fed is uniquely positioned to do something about it."
Read more: How jobs, inflation, and the Fed are all related
Beyond the Cook dispute, the new Senate majority will dictate the Fed's long-term leadership.
While natural turnover on the Board of Governors for 14-year terms is historically slow, key institutional shifts are looming. There is only one governor whose term ends in the next two years — Jay Powell's in January 2028. As a result of the election, the administration will now need to replace Powell with someone amenable to Senate Democrats, or else leave the seat vacant. Vice Chair Philip Jefferson's term as vice chair ends in September, though he could remain as a governor.
In the near term, the political shift provides breathing room for current Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, Trump's hand-picked appointee.
RSM economist Joseph Brusuelas deemed Warsh one of the big winners of the election.
"One gets the sense that the administration will have other priorities over the next two years," Brusuelas wrote on X. "Warsh and the Fed will be free to pursue price stability and shaping policy in the best interests of the economy rather than the incumbent."
But Feroli warned that if Warsh wants to remain Fed chair beyond one term, which ends in May 2030, he should begin courting the new legislative majority.
"While there's another election between now and then, last night increased the odds his term will end with Democratic control of the Senate," Feroli said. "Unless he wants to be a one-term chair, Warsh will need to spend less time looking out the window and more time walking the halls of Congress."

articles.title_zh: China’s Yutong Bus expands overseas as new-energy bus exports surge
articles.content_orig:
‘Overseas public transport demand is growing fast, and international buyers are seeking more premium electric buses,’ Asia-Pacific CEO says
China’s Yutong Bus, the world’s largest electric bus manufacturer, is seeing its overseas shipments climb steadily, with demand growing rapidly in countries such as Australia, Malaysia, Saudi Arabia and Morocco.
Based in Zhengzhou in central China’s Henan province, the company now generates more than half of its total revenue from overseas sales. New-energy models – comprising pure-electric and hybrid vehicles – have made up 25 per cent of its bus exports so far this year, a sharp increase from just 3 per cent in 2018.
Yutong holds more than 10 per cent of the global market, including China, for large and medium-sized buses and coaches, according to the company. Its competitors include domestic peers BYD, Zhongtong Bus and Xiamen King Long United Automotive Industry, as well as overseas companies like Mercedes-Benz and Volvo.

articles.title_orig: Sudan, Ethiopia shut each other’s consulates in tit-for-tat move: Reports
articles.title_zh: Sudan, Ethiopia shut each other’s consulates in tit-for-tat move: Reports
articles.content_orig:
Sudan has closed Ethiopia’s consulate near their shared border and expelled its diplomats, hours after Addis Ababa expelled six Sudanese diplomats and shut down Khartoum’s consulate in the region, according to media reports.
Ethiopian and Sudanese officials told the Reuters and AFP news agencies about the tit-for-tat moves on Wednesday, as tensions continue to rise between the two countries. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity.
Sudan accuses Ethiopia of aiding the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a Sudanese paramilitary group embroiled in a civil war against the country’s regular army.
Ethiopia, meanwhile, accuses Sudan of backing rebels the government in Addis Ababa is fighting in the northern ⁠Tigray region.
The allegations and counter-allegations, which both sides deny, have raised fears that the two conflicts could bleed into each other, spawning a broader war in the Horn of Africa.
Reuters, citing a senior official, reported that Ethiopia ordered six staff members of the Sudanese consulate in the border town ⁠of Asosa to leave within 48 hours. It said the official asked not to be named so he could discuss a sensitive diplomatic matter.
The Associated Press news agency also reported the action, citing an Ethiopian intelligence official. It said a Sudanese official had corroborated the expulsions, adding that Ethiopian authorities summoned Sudan’s ambassador on Sunday to announce the consulate’s closure.
The Sudanese official said the staff departed on Tuesday evening. The agency said neither official had provided a specific reason for the ousters.
In retaliation, Sudan’s government closed the Ethiopian consulate in the eastern city of Gadarif and expelled the diplomats working there, two Sudanese officials told Reuters on Wednesday.
An official separately told AFP that Sudan responded by “informing the staff of the Ethiopian consulate in Gadarif”, near the border, “that they were persona non grata, and gave them 48 hours to leave the country”.
The expulsions came after ⁠Sudan lodged a complaint against Ethiopia with both the United Nations Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council on Sunday, accusing Ethiopia of allowing the RSF to use its territory to launch deadly drone attacks against civilian infrastructure in Sudan.
“The Sudanese government remains committed to its right to defend its territory. Nevertheless, it is making ⁠every possible effort to avoid an open war with Ethiopia,” said Amjad Farid, political and foreign affairs adviser for Sudan’s Transitional Sovereign Council. The Sudanese council is the country’s internationally recognised collective head of state.
A direct military confrontation with Addis Ababa would severely strain an already exhausted Sudanese military apparatus, which is still involved in intense battles with the RSF in the southeast of the country.
Addis Ababa denies it supports the RSF in Sudan’s civil war.
The fighting between Sudan’s military and the RSF, which erupted in 2023, has since killed tens of thousands of people and displaced more than 14 million. The civil war has created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, according to the UN.
On Sunday, drone strikes on electricity substations in the northern Sudanese towns of al-Dabba and Abu Hamad knocked out power. Sudan’s government and the rights group Emergency Lawyers blamed the RSF.
The conflict has more widely disrupted electricity and water supplies and threatened essential medical services.
Ethiopia’s order on the Sudanese diplomats also follows its decision to expel 10 Eritrean diplomats and close Addis Ababa’s embassy in Eritrea on October 1. Eritrea responded by severing diplomatic ties.
Ethiopia also expelled an Egyptian diplomat last month. Relations with Cairo have long been strained over Ethiopia’s massive dam on the Blue Nile, which Egypt fears could threaten its water supplies.
Addis Ababa has accused Sudan, Egypt and Eritrea of supporting Tigrayan rebels who launched an offensive against Ethiopian government forces in September. All three countries have denied the accusations.

articles.title_orig: Palestine Action ban undermined confidence in anti-terror laws, Supreme Court told
articles.title_zh: Palestine Action ban undermined confidence in anti-terror laws, Supreme Court told
articles.content_orig:
The banning of Palestine Action has led to a "crisis in confidence" in the UK's anti-terrorism laws and triggered unprecedented civil disobedience from law-abiding protesters, the Supreme Court has been told.
Opening a major legal challenge to the group's proscription last year, lawyers for co-founder Huda Ammori said that no other protest organisation had been treated the same way.
They told the five justices that the UK's highest court had never before had to consider whether banning a group under terrorism legislation was compatible with freedom of speech and protest.
Twenty-seven protesters were arrested outside the Supreme Court on Wednesday as the hearing took place, the Metropolitan Police said.
Lawyers for Ammori told the court that thousands of elderly people, many veterans of other radical causes, had been arrested for holding up signs supportive of the group since its proscription.
Home Office figures seen by the BBC indicate that there have been more than 4,000 arrests so far at protests in which people have held up signs supportive of the group.
In practice, many demonstrators have been arrested more than once, with 1,200 charges authorised by prosecutors to date. Those trials are in limbo until the outcome of this case.
Henry Blaxland KC told the court that "far from depriving Palestine Action of the oxygen of publicity" and "far from discrediting its brand", proscription of the group has had the opposite effect.
"All it's done is to pour fuel on to a fire of one of the most publicly-contested issues of our time," he said.
"It was disproportionate to do that and in my submission completely unnecessary."
During often tense exchanges with the judges, Ammori's team accepted that Palestine Action could not be described as an ordinary and peaceful protest group.
They said that its members had carried out "direct action" protests by occupying or vandalising firms linked to Israel's military - with only three of 385 incidents assessed by the Home Secretary as constituting an offence under the Terrorism Act.
The UK's definition of terrorism includes incidents of serious damage to property for a cause - and at least two break-ins at defence firms have been described in criminal courts as having caused millions in damage.
Raza Husain KC, for Ammori, said that the judges had to put aside allegations of criminality - for which the state had many powers - and consider whether the Home Secretary's decision to label the group as terrorists had been disproportionate.
"Palestine Action was proscribed on the basis of less than one per cent of its actions over five years assessed as falling within the outer limits of a definition of terrorism," he said.
"The Home Secretary's own experts confirmed the vast majority of its direct action would not constitute an act of terrorism on the basis that any damage to property is typically more minor. Common tactics include graffiti, petty vandalism, occupation, and lock-ons."
One Palestine Action member has been convicted and jailed of fracturing a police officer's back with a sledgehammer - but the court was told that the group had never advocated such violence.
The Supreme Court has received arguments from free speech campaigners, arguing the ban interferes with the right to protest.
But another submission from a coalition of Jewish groups argued that Palestine Action was a "sinister" organisation intent on attacking its community interests.
"The Court of Appeal [following earlier hearings] rightly concluded that PA is a violent organisation concerned in terrorism with a wide range of targets," said Adam Wagner KC in written submissions for the Jewish communal groups.
He continued: "Its activities are often undertaken covertly with no suggestion of restraint or proportionality, and that at the point it was proscribed it had an escalating trajectory of seriousness and an expanding focus."
Wagner said Palestine Action's "crosshairs" had moved from targeting Elbit, a defence firm with an Israeli parent company, to "figures or institutions deemed by PA to be 'Zionist'".
"Because most British Jews and Jewish institutions have a connection with Israel, a campaign against institutions PA's activists consider to be 'complicit' with Israel is, in practice, a campaign that threatens the mainstream Jewish community," he said.
However, Jewish Bloc, a group that campaigns in solidarity with Palestinians, told has also written to the court to say that claims that PA targeted their community were a "fundamental misrepresentation of the underlying evidence".
Rachel Scott KC, for the organisation, told the justices: "Neither the Jewish Leadership Council (JLC) nor the Community Security Trust (CST) have any democratic mandate. Claims that either organisation can be viewed as the voice of British Jews must therefore be viewed with very significant caution.
"The framing of PA as an organisation which threatened and intimidated 'the Jewish Community' is demonstrably false and a deliberate elision. The evidence instead shows that it targeted entities, organisations and institutions  with an established link to Israel's illegal activities against the Palestinian people."
The case continues on Thursday with a judgment expected at a later date.

The I nstitute for the Study of War (ISW) and The Critical Threats Project (CTP) at the American Enterprise Institute are publishing updates Monday through Friday to provide analysis on the war with Iran and the broader Middle East. Weekday updates cover events from the past 24-hour period, whereas weekend updates are abbreviated and cover the Houthi-Saudi conflict and major breaking developments related to the war with Iran.
Recent Houthi advances in Lahij Governorate are part of a Houthi campaign designed to confront the internationally recognized government of Yemen with simultaneous dilemmas in order to undermine its ability to prioritize and respond to threats on multiple fronts. The Houthis captured mountainous positions in al Maqatirah District on November 2 that provide Houthi forces with high ground that overlooks Tur al Bahah District, which sits between Taiz Governorate’s rugged, mountainous terrain and the coastal plain leading to Aden City. [i] Geolocated footage indicates that Houthi forces likely advanced southeastward from Hayjat al Abd and captured Souq al Roubah on November 1, which is located at a key crossroads leading north into al Shamayatayn District. [ii] Geolocated footage posted on November 2 also indicates that Houthi forces then advanced further south from Souq al Roubah and captured Jabal Irf. [iii] Jabal Irf overlooks the last government-controlled sections of the Taiz-Aden ground line of communication (GLOC). Houthi positions in this area could enable the Houthis to establish fire control over Yemeni government-aligned reinforcements transiting north along the GLOC.
Houthi advances in the direction of Aden are part of a broader Houthi campaign that is designed to confront the Yemeni government with competing demands for its forces and resources across multiple fronts. The Houthis’ establishment of positions in al Maqatirah District and ability to advance south threatens Aden City, and as such, are likely designed to impose a dilemma on government forces on whether to divert forces from other fronts and efforts. Government forces in southwestern Yemen are currently fighting against the Houthis around Taiz City in an effort to break the Houthi encirclement of Taiz City and along the Red Sea coastal front in order to recapture territory near the Bab al Mandeb.
Houthi advances into al Maqatirah District since October 30 are threatening government reinforcement and resupply routes on multiple fronts, for example. The Houthis likely aim to seize additional sections of the Taiz-Aden GLOC, which also sets conditions for the Houthis to besiege or capture Aden City in the future, if they choose to do so. [iv] Additional Houthi control of the Taiz-Aden GLOC would also further isolate government-aligned forces encircled in Taiz City and constrain the government’s ability to reinforce its positions across the region.
Houthi advances in al Maqatirah also threaten government positions along the Red Sea coastal plain. Houthi forces may also attempt to outflank and isolate government-aligned forces on the Red Sea coastal front by advancing towards the Mokha-Taiz GLOC, which supplies government-aligned forces operating on that front. Such an advance would compound the pressure on government-aligned forces by threatening both their positions on the Red Sea coast and the routes needed to sustain them. Houthi forces would likely face the same vulnerabilities to air attacks in lowland terrain that could constrain any theoretical advance toward Aden, however.
The Yemeni government has already diverted forces from the coastal plain to meet the Houthi threat in al Maqatirah, which underscores the dilemmas imposed by the Houthis’ campaign. The Yemeni government reportedly redeployed an unspecified number of Red Sea coast-based Southern Giants Brigades and Homeland Shield Forces units to al Maqatirah District on November 2, likely to contain the Houthi advance. [v] These forces have previously helped halt Houthi advances along the Red Sea coastal plain since the Houthi offensive began in September 2026. [vi] Their redeployment could weaken the government's defense on the coastal plain, depending on the size and characteristics of the units deployed. The recent appointments of several new commanders to the al Maqatirah area, including a commander of the government-aligned Homeland Shield Forces, also indicates Yemeni government concern about Houthi advancs in al Maqatirah. [vii]
The Houthis’ current efforts to capture Taiz City further compound the Yemeni government’s competing operational demands as Houthi advances in al Maqatirah District threaten to draw government forces away from efforts to break the encirclement of Taiz City. Yemeni government-aligned forces and civilians in Taiz City are facing food, fuel, medicine, and other resource shortages after the Houthis severed the last Yemeni government ground lines of communication (GLOC) into central Taiz Governorate on October 6. [viii] The Houthis’ continued encirclement of the city and control over major roads in the area limit the government’s ability to maneuver across southwestern Yemen while permitting the Houthis to carry a high volume of forces and supplies north toward Taiz City along more established roadways. Yemeni government forces encircled in Taiz City reportedly launched counterattacks into al Misrakh District, Taiz Governorate, on November 2, possibly in response to the Houthi advances in al Maqatirah. [ix]
The Houthis may struggle to sustain advances south toward the coastal plain if the Yemeni government receives sufficient air and military support. The terrain south of Tur al Bahah would expose Houthi forces to greater risk from air attack given that lowland terrain south of Tur al Bahah offers less terrain protection than the mountainous positions Houthi forces currently occupy in al Maqatirah District. Government-aligned forces, supported by air assets, have previously halted Houthi attempts to capture remaining government-held areas of the Red Sea coastal plain and the Bab al Mandeb Strait since September 10. [x] These setbacks suggest that Houthi forces may struggle to consolidate their gains in exposed terrain, particularly if government-aligned forces can sustain air support and reinforce threatened positions. The Houthis’ ability to exploit their current high ground will therefore depend in part on whether they can advance south before government-aligned forces establish effective defensive positions. The Houthis may nevertheless achieve a broader operational effect even if they fail to advance further south. Continued Houthi advances could force the government to divert additional forces from Taiz and the Red Sea coastal fronts, disrupt reinforcement and resupply routes, and weaken its ability to respond to Houthi offensives elsewhere.

articles.title_orig: Israel’s Herzog accepts vote results, opens talks on forming a government
articles.title_zh: Israel’s Herzog accepts vote results, opens talks on forming a government
articles.content_orig:
Netanyahu: letting Arab parties into gov’t will ‘dismantle’ Israel
Israel’s President Isaac Herzog has accepted the certified results of last week’s parliamentary elections and begun consultations with party leaders on whom to task with forming the next government.
The moves on Wednesday dealt a blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s efforts to discredit the vote, in which he and his allies lost their majority in the 120-member parliament, while Arab-led parties made historic gains.
“The elections are over. Now is the time to face reality,” Herzog said.
In the October 27 vote, neither Netanyahu’s coalition nor the bloc of his chief rival, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, secured the 61 seats required to govern. The prime minister’s coalition won 53, while Eisonkot’s got 48.
That leaves open the possibility of an alliance between the two men or an alliance between Eisenkot and the Arab-led parties – Ra’am and the Joint List – which had secured a record 19 seats.
Herzog concluded the first day of consultations with party leaders on Wednesday night, and said talks would continue on Thursday.
On Wednesday, the president said he met with representatives of the Religious Zionism and Zehut, Shas, and Yisrael Beytenu factions. He “received their recommendations regarding the identity of the Knesset member upon whom the task of forming the government should be assigned,” Herzog said on X.
Three factions aligned with Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist base recommended that the prime minister be given a chance to form a coalition, while a fourth, led by a former Netanyahu ally turned rival, backed Eisenkot.
Eight more parties, including the two Arab-led factions, are scheduled to meet with the president on Thursday, with Eisenkot’s Yashar party and Netanyahu’s Likud going last.
Eisenkot’s prospects improved when Ra’am, a major Arab-led party, said it would recommend him. That brought his expected support to 56 lawmakers, according to the Israeli news site Ynet, which is still short of a majority.
The other Arab-led party, the Joint List, has not announced its position. Israel’s Channel 12 reported that the party was expected to coordinate with Eisenkot, endorsing him if asked or abstaining if he preferred. Its 11 seats could push him past 61.
Netanyahu’s 53-seat bloc, by contrast, may not yield 53 endorsements.
Degel HaTorah, which holds four of United Torah Judaism’s seven seats, said it would recommend neither candidate. The ultra-Orthodox faction broke with Netanyahu over his coalition’s failure to pass legislation exempting Haredi men from military service, The Times of Israel reported.
Once the consultations end, Herzog will choose the candidate he considers best placed to assemble a coalition, almost certainly Netanyahu or Eisenkot. He has several days to announce his decision, after which the nominee will have 28 days to form a government, with a possible 14-day extension.
If neither man succeeds, Israel would hold another election early next year.
Netanyahu and his supporters meanwhile have repeatedly made unsubstantiated claims that the Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, possibly with foreign assistance.
But Israel’s elections commission said earlier on Wednesday that it had conducted a thorough investigation of all parties’ claims of fraud and found “no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results”.
Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara also rejected a request to question elected officials without supporting evidence.
Herzog urged both camps to compromise to avoid a new election, saying they must accept that “not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled”.
“In the current reality, in which there is no clear winner after the elections, I ask for originality and creativity, courage and goodwill, so that the State of Israel emerges the winner,” he said.
He also backed investigating the suspected interference but warned against smearing Palestinian-Israeli voters, saying he had “great respect” for Israel’s Palestinian minority, which makes up about 20 percent of the population.
“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Ten years of the Paris Agreement: Has the world kept its climate promises?
articles.title_zh: Ten years of the Paris Agreement: Has the world kept its climate promises?
articles.content_orig:
Ten years ago, the Paris Agreement entered into force, binding nearly every country to a shared goal: to hold global warming well below 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) above preindustrial levels and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5C (2.7F).
A decade on, the deal has helped drive stronger climate policies and a rapid expansion of clean energy. But emissions remain near record highs, temperatures keep climbing and countries are still far from the cuts needed to keep a 1.5C limit within reach.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at what the Paris Agreement set out to do, how far global temperatures have risen since and which countries are driving emissions.
The Paris Agreement is a legally binding climate treaty adopted by 196 parties at the United Nations climate summit in Paris, also known as COP21, on December 12, 2015. It entered into force on November 4, 2016.
The United States, the world’s second-largest greenhouse gas emitter after China, has joined and left the agreement twice. President Donald Trump ordered both withdrawals. The first took effect in November 2020, and President Joe Biden rejoined in February 2021. The US left again in January this year, 12 months after Trump ordered its exit for a second time.
Today, 194 parties, 193 countries and the European Union, belong to the agreement.
Rather than imposing the same cuts on everyone, the agreement asks each government to set its own targets through nationally determined contributions, or NDCs, outlining how it will cut emissions and adapt to climate change.
Countries submit a new, more ambitious NDC every five years, and a Global Stocktake assesses collective progress on the same cycle. The agreement also covers reporting, climate finance and support for developing countries.
The agreement does not force countries to meet their targets. It relies on transparency and international pressure to raise ambition.
Temperatures have kept rising since the deal was adopted.
In 2024, the planet was more than 1.5C warmer than preindustrial levels across a full calendar year for the first time.
The past three years, 2023 to 2025, were the hottest on record and the first three-year period to average more than 1.5C of warming.
The long-term warming average now stands at about 1.4C, and scientists expect it to surpass 1.5C around the end of this decade.
In October, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) said the chance of keeping warming to 1.5C without overshooting it has been lost.
“Every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5C increases climate impacts and risks, such as the deadly floods, heatwaves and wildfires that have plagued many nations this year,” UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen said.
Still, the outlook is less bleak than it was in 2015.
When the Paris Agreement was signed, existing policies put the world on course for about 3.6C of warming by 2100. According to the Climate Action Tracker , that projection has since fallen to about 2.6C as countries adopted climate policies and clean energy expanded.
Progress has stalled since 2021, however, and current policies still point to far more warming than the agreement promised.
Carbon dioxide, the main driver of warming, comes mostly from burning coal, oil and natural gas while deforestation removes trees that once absorbed it.
China, the US and India now produce more than half of the world’s annual emissions. China alone emits more than the US, India, Russia and Japan combined although the US has released the most carbon emissions historically.
Investments in clean energy are now almost double those in fossil fuels, but emission cuts have been too slow to keep 1.5C within reach.
The graphic below ranks the biggest emitters in 2024 and shows how their emissions have changed since the agreement took effect in 2016.
China remains by far the largest polluter, and its emissions have kept rising alongside those of India and Indonesia as these fast-growing economies burn more coal to meet soaring power demand. Indonesia has climbed into the top 10, replacing Canada.
Germany, Japan and the US have cut their emissions, largely by replacing coal with renewables and gas. But growth elsewhere has outweighed those cuts, and global emissions are 9 percent higher than in 2016.

articles.title_orig: France: Cyberattack targets blood bank refrigerators
articles.title_zh: France: Cyberattack targets blood bank refrigerators
articles.content_orig:
Blood banks in France were included among cyberattacks that hit refrigeration systems in several European countries on Sunday and Monday, French authorities said on Wednesday.
The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said that a " cybersecurity incident" targeted a refrigeration service provider affecting control systems at three cold storage sites for plasma and blood samples.
The cyberattack attempted to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but it was warded off before any damage could be done. The plasma in the affected refrigerators was transferred or secured, the EFS said.
"No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost," the EFS said in a statement, adding that its distribution operations were not interrupted.
The cyberattack was first reported on Wednesday by the French weekly newspaper Le Canard Enchaine , which said the temperatures had been programmed to reach a boiling 110 C (230 F), rather than -30 Celsius (minus 22 Fahrenheit).
"Monitoring and alarm systems quickly detected the anomalies, allowing staff to take action to ensure that no blood products or samples were compromised," the EFS said.
France's cybersecurity agency and Health Ministry said an investigation is underway, but did not indicate who could have been responsible.
The Health Ministry said Wednesday that remote access to the affected refrigerators was disabled, and credited monitoring and alarm systems with ensuring the safety of blood supplies.
Coolworld, the company supplying the refrigeration equipment, said the vulnerability was related to a component from a "third-party supplier and was outside Coolworld's direct control."
On Sunday and Monday, a cyberattack targeted refrigeration systems at supermarkets in several European countries, including France and Germany, destroying large quantities of frozen food.
It was reminiscent of a similar attack three weeks ago targeting refrigeration systems at dozens of French supermarkets.
The attacks have cost supermarkets millions of euros in wasted food.
On Wednesday, Dutch supermarket chain Ahold Delhaize said it expects the cyberattack in October to reduce quarterly sales by as much as €250 million ($281 million).
"While most of the disruption was contained within two weeks, work continues to fully restore our normal operations," CEO Franz Muller said.

articles.title_orig: Altar Stone mystery continues as theory overturned
articles.title_zh: Altar Stone mystery continues as theory overturned
articles.content_orig:
A new study exploring the origins of the six tonne Altar Stone at Stonehenge has ruled out a theory that it came from an area of Scotland.
The 4.9 metre sandstone slab within the circle was initially believed to have originated in Wales until a more recent study pointed towards it coming from north east Scotland.
Scientific tests were carried out in the Orcadian Basin area of Scotland, but researchers failed to find a location with the same characteristics of the stone in that area.
However study lead, Professor Duncan Pirrie from the University of South Wales, said the latest investigation has left them "far better equipped to focus on the areas most likely to yield an answer."
Pirrie said his latest publication on the Altar Stone has "built the clearest picture yet" and was "the most comprehensive geological investigation of the Altar Stone ever undertaken".
Professor Nick Pearce from Aberystwyth University, who worked on the previous research, said "ruling out potential source areas is just as important as identifying new ones".
The geochemistry expert said: "Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the Altar Stone originated.
"The stone is unique among those at Stonehenge, and tracing its source would provide valuable new insights into its remarkable journey to Salisbury Plain thousands of years ago."
The world-famous Wiltshire monument was constructed in multiple phases over thousands of years, between 3000 and 1600 BC. However, not all stones come from the area.
The smaller bluestones travelled around 225km from west Wales with research suggesting a few were taken directly from another circle.
The latest study combined new observations and looked at fragments of the stone in museum collections, examining structure, minerals and composition.
It has been published in the Journal of the Geological Society.

articles.title_orig: Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger found dead in Berlin hotel
articles.title_zh: Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger found dead in Berlin hotel
articles.content_orig:
Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger was found dead in a hotel in Berlin on Wednesday, the German capital's public prosecutor's office said.
Aiwanger was Bavaria's deputy premier, economy minister and the chairman of the right-wing populist Free Voters party. He was 55 years old.
The circumstances surrounding Aiwanger's death are still unclear. Police and prosecutors in the German capital have launched an investigation.
On Wednesday evening, investigators said the goal is to "determine the specific cause of death and the circumstances surrounding it, as well as to rule out any possible foul play."
Aiwanger had been feeling unwell on Wednesday, German tabloid Bild reported.
He was scheduled to deliver a speech at the opening of a party office in Berlin but canceled his appearance for health reasons, German news agency dpa reported.
Aiwanger's body was found on Wednesday evening at the "Neuer Fritz" Hotel on Friedrichstrasse in Berlin-Mitte, according to Bild .
Bavarian state premier, the Christian Social Union 's Markus Söder, has said he is "deeply shocked" by the news of his deputy's death.
"The sudden death of Hubert Aiwanger is an absolute tragedy," Söder said in a post on X.
"Our thoughts are now first and foremost with his family and his children. We mourn with them and pray for them."
Born in Lower Bavaria in southern Germany , Aiwanger was elected to the Bavarian State Parliament in 2008 with the Free Voters and became their parliamentary group leader.
Since 2018, his party has been in a coalition with the center-right CSU, the Bavarian sister party of the ruling Christian Democratic Union (CDU) . Aiwanger served as the state's Minister of Economic Affairs and deputy premier.
Aiwanger was the face of the Free Voters in Bavaria and across Germany, and was known for his combative approach.
But his political success in the state did not translate to the national level, as the Free Voters never won enough seats to enter the Bundestag , Germany's federal parliament.
In the weeks before state elections in 2023, Aiwanger became embroiled in a national scandal when the Süddeutsche Zeitung reported that he had written an antisemitic leaflet during high school in the 1980s, which included references to Nazi-era atrocities such as Auschwitz.
He is survived by two children. He was not married but lived with Tanja Schweiger, a district administrator for the Free Voters.

articles.title_orig: Joshua Wong, Hong Kong Democracy Activist, Is Sentenced to 10 Years in Prison
articles.title_zh: Joshua Wong, Hong Kong Democracy Activist, Is Sentenced to 10 Years in Prison
articles.content_orig:
Joshua Wong, once a teenage figurehead of Hong Kong’s democracy movement, faces the prospect of entering middle age in prison, after a court Thursday meted out a 10-year sentence over a second national security conviction.
Wong became a prominent activist when he was a teenager, and entered prison for the first time at 23. He turned 30 last month.
In September, he pleaded guilty to conspiring with fellow activists to invite foreign sanctions against China and Hong Kong in 2020 – the year Beijing introduced the city’s National Security Law (NSL), which led to a crackdown on dissent, the shuttering of vocal news outlets, and the dissolution of civic groups.
Wong is already serving 4 years and 8 months in prison, after pleading guilty in a landmark subversion trial in 2024. He was due for release in January.
Beijing imposed the NSL on Hong Kong after huge and often violent pro-democracy protests convulsed the international financial hub in 2019.
The law tightened Beijing’s grip on the former British colony. Both the Hong Kong and Chinese governments say it has helped restore stability, but rights groups say the law has stifled dissent and made any criticism of the government risky.
Calling Wong’s case “grave,” Judge William Tam said the activist conspired with others – including Nathan Law, a former legislator now living in self-exile overseas – to call for foreign sanctions at a time when Hong Kong was dealing with its own social turmoil, referring to the anti-government protests.
After the NSL came in, the judge said, Wong and his conspirators “continued to promote such calls not only through their own social media accounts but also via prominent news media or outlets in the West, reaching both local and international audience.”
“Whilst it is a very heavy sentence on the defendant, the punishment must fit the gravity of the crime committed,” he said, adding that it’s “also necessary for this court to express the community’s abhorrence” at Wong’s actions.
In his mitigation letter, viewed by CNN, Wong wrote that his activism “was never driven by hatred.”
He’s been spending his spare time in jail studying the law and keeping abreast of technological advances, including artificial intelligence, he said.
“Yet none of my aspirations for the future is more important than my solemn wish to care for my ageing parents once I complete my sentence,” he wrote.
China’s leaders have previously labeled Wong and other activists “separatists.”
In the latest case, prosecutors accused Wong of conspiring with others to lobby the United States and other countries to sanction China and Hong Kong, prior to the NSL’s imposition.
This, they said, happened through social media campaigning, as well as meetings with US politicians, including former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and then Senator Marco Rubio, now the US secretary of state.
The lobbying continued after the law was enacted, prosecutors said, with the US sanctioning more than a dozen Hong Kong and Chinese officials after 2020.
A Hong Kong government spokesperson earlier dismissed international criticism of Wong’s prosecution.
“The lawful exercise of free speech must not be conflated with taking actions to collude with a foreign country to impose ‘sanctions’ to harm one’s own country,” they said in September.
Speaking after the sentence was announced, Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee, a former top security official, said Wong and Law committed “extremely serious offences, which not only severely undermined national sovereignty, security, and development interests, but also directly prejudiced the well-being of the general public and the stability of society.”
Ahead of the sentencing Thursday morning, police had heightened security outside the court near Hong Kong’s financial district, where dozens of people had camped out – some for two nights – to catch a glimpse of one of the city’s most famous prisoners.
Among them was housewife ET Wong, who said she had started following Wong’s campaigning when he was still an adolescent.
“He chose a difficult path for the future, human rights and student movements of Hong Kong,” she said. “He should not have been in jail for one single day.”
Activist Lui Yuk-lin held a card with Wong’s name on it as she entered the building, lamenting the fate of the former teen figurehead.
“He’s a child in my heart,” she said.
When he was led into court, Wong, wearing a navy shirt and his usual black-framed glasses, nodded to supporters in the public gallery. Given the limited space, well-wishers took turns filing through the gallery.
Weeks after pleading guilty to his second national security charge in September, Wong – who’s been behind bars since 2020 – told his friend in a letter that he had been feeling “so-so.”
“[It’s] very difficult to describe the feeling and thought,” Wong wrote in the letter, shared with CNN by his friend.
But the former activist also encouraged his friend to stay positive, citing a verse from the Bible.
“There is no fear in love,” Wong wrote, quoting from The First Epistle of John, adding that the fear he had experienced over the past few years made him appreciate his love for his friends and the city even more.
Louis Lee, who shared his exchanges with Wong, said they discussed everything from music to their favourite Japanese anime, and would reminiscence about good times.
Reading Wong’s letters sometimes brought Lee to tears.
“As a friend, I miss him so much and I long to see the day when he’s out of the prison,” Lee said.
The skinny, bespectacled activist with a knack for fiery public speaking rose to prominence in 2012 at the age of 15, leading sit-in protests with his friends to successfully overturn a government plan to introduce Chinese civic education to the city’s schools.
At the time, critics feared the proposed curriculum amounted to propaganda by Beijing. Under the NSL, it’s now compulsory in every school.
Two years later, Wong became one of the key leaders of the city’s Umbrella Movement protests that rallied thousands of predominantly young people to the streets to call for greater democracy by blocking major thoroughfares for 79 straight days.
In 2016, he co-founded pro-democracy party Demosisto, which successfully sent co-founder Law to the city’s Legislative Council as its youngest member (Wong was too young to run.) The party announced its disbandment hours after Beijing passed the NSL, with Law revealing days later he had left Hong Kong.
Law is now one of dozens of democracy activists overseas wanted by Hong Kong’s national security police, and who have had a cash bounty put on them.
Authorities disqualified Wong when he tried to run again in 2020. He was later arrested and charged along with dozens of others for taking part in unofficial primaries held to screen candidates for Legislative Council elections.
In what was widely known as the “47 case,” after the number of opposition figures on trial, prosecutors said Wong and others subverted the Hong Kong government in 2020 by engaging in a primary election – a common practice in many democracies.
At the time, Hong Kong authorities said the primary vote was a “vicious plot” intended to “paralyze the government and undermine state power,” and accused those who took part of intending to use their mandate to block legislation indiscriminately.
Of the 47, most pleaded guilty while 14 were convicted and sentenced to up to 10 years in prison, after a 2024 trial that marked the single largest prosecution of pro-democracy activists under the NSL. Two were acquitted.
Since the NSL came into effect, civil groups have disbanded, and some independent media outlets have been shut down. The city’s legislature now comprises only pro-Beijing loyalists, while most pro-democracy figures are either in jail or in exile overseas.

articles.title_orig: How India Can Manage Chinese Surpluses
articles.title_zh: How India Can Manage Chinese Surpluses
articles.content_orig:
By Thomas Asplund-Meineckem , William B. Smith, and  Shiro Armstrong
China’s resurgent trade surplus has revived fears across developing Asia that it is pulling up the ladder of export-led industrialization behind it. In New Delhi, India’s bilateral trade deficit with China — over $112 billion in 2025–26 — is being read as the result of unfair Chinese competition and domestic structural weakness, both cited as grounds for protection. But viewing China primarily as a competitor misses its potentially complementary role and the case for managing the relationship rather than retreating from it.
Concerns over a ‘China squeeze’ hold that China has industrialized without ceding labor-intensive industries, partly due to its industrial policies and structurally undervalued renminbi. The argument goes that Chinese goods undercut developing countries’ firms at home and outcompete them in third markets, while China demands few of their exports, leaving developing countries little room to industrialize.
New Delhi has been especially receptive to this argument, framing economic engagement with China as a threat to be contained. In thinly veiled comments directed at China in June 2026, Minister of External Affairs Subrahmanyam Jaishankar argued that ‘the right to industrialize, indeed the capacity to do so, is being denied’ to many developing countries.
Convinced that its firms cannot compete with China on fair terms, New Delhi has turned its trade policy inwards . India has increased tariffs since 2018 to an average of around 17.6 percent, among the highest in Asia, and raised non-tariff barriers. In November 2019, India also walked out of Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) negotiations, largely over concerns it would expose Indian firms and farmers to a surge of cheap Chinese imports. But this ‘ RCEP minus China ’ strategy leaves India outside the regional production networks deeply integrated with China.
Underlying this strategy is concern about India’s bilateral trade deficit. But economies tend to run deficits with countries that supply their inputs and surpluses with those that buy their outputs. Imports of this kind reflect complementarities between economies, and by lowering costs, make local firms more productive and competitive.
China is above all a supplier to Indian manufacturing. Capital goods, machinery and intermediate goods accounted for around 87 percent of Indian imports from China in 2024.
India’s pharmaceutical and electronics industries show the value of integration into Chinese value chains. Between 2015 and 2022, Indian value added in electronics exports nearly tripled as their Chinese content rose sixfold. In pharmaceuticals, it rose by half as Chinese content doubled.
Labor-intensive industries like textiles show a similar pattern. With China moving upstream out of garment assembly, Bangladesh and Vietnam have taken substantial market share. But India’s share of global textile exports has remained stagnant at around 3 percent , with its garment makers paying higher duties on imported fabric.
Tariff and non-tariff barriers to Chinese inputs shelter upstream firms but raise costs for downstream exporters who compete with Chinese exports in foreign markets regardless. Input tariff neutrality would help Indian firms integrate into global value chains, raising domestic value added in absolute terms even if the foreign value-added share of exports rises.
Deeper integration would also help India sell more to China. Despite supplying almost 17 percent of India’s imports in 2025–26, China bought only 4.4 percent of India’s exports. Part of the gap reflects Chinese barriers in key Indian sectors, but Indian firms also struggle to match Chinese rivals on cost and scale.
Indian protectionism against China will not resolve the distortions imposed by Chinese overcapacity . At best, India’s barriers offset some of their effects — but raise costs for Indian firms. India can gain more from importing cheaper Chinese equipment, green technology and productive capacity for its own industrialization — especially given unilateral action will not change the policies driving China’s surpluses.
Genuine Chinese distortions demand a collective response through international and regional agreements. RCEP’s joint committees and ministerial meetings allow members to press Beijing on unfair practices, and its standards and customs chapters provide channels to raise the approval delays preventing Indian goods from reaching Chinese markets.
Membership would also pull India into regional production networks. RCEP’s common rules of origin make it easier to spread production across member economies, since inputs from any member count towards origin, qualifying the final good for preferential tariffs across the bloc. RCEP also provides safeguards against damaging import surges, allowing members to suspend tariff cuts or raise duties when imports injure domestic industries.
RCEP members remain open to India’s accession — New Delhi could take up an observer seat now and apply to join without the waiting period other applicants face. The agreement’s first General Review in 2027 offers a natural moment to negotiate entry.
The Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) offers further avenues for managing Chinese surpluses. China’s application to join — pending since September 2021 — offers the region leverage, holding out access to CPTPP markets in return for reform of state-owned enterprises, investment and government procurement.
The same logic applies to India, for which CPTPP membership is a longer-term goal. Its regulatory disciplines would demand reforms India’s political economy has long resisted. A staged process — beginning with a gap analysis and cooperation in less contentious areas before negotiating transition periods and carve-outs for sensitive sectors — would give policymakers time to build domestic support for reform.
Indian policymakers should understand China not only as a competitor but as a potential complementor. The trade deficit driving India inwards largely consists of inputs that make its firms more productive and competitive. Unilateral protection and absence from RCEP and CPTPP leave India outside the production networks that would allow its manufacturing sector to prosper, and without a voice to press genuine concerns. Managing the relationship through regional arrangements offers a surer way up the ladder of export-led industrialization than going it alone.

articles.title_orig: Russia, China may be more aggressive if they feel Trump is on "his way out": Brookings
articles.title_zh: Russia, China may be more aggressive if they feel Trump is on "his way out": Brookings
articles.content_orig:
Russia and China could become more aggressive over the next two years if they conclude that President Donald Trump is politically weakened and on "his way out" after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, Brookings Institution senior fellow Robert Kagan told CNBC.
Speaking on " Squawk Box Asia ," Kagan said the war with Iran had also exposed how Washington has "proved itself rather incapable militarily" in terms of capacity, which would be critical in Asia.
"Everybody can see how much our stocks are depleted in terms of interceptors and missiles, which are of vital interest in the Asian theater," he said.
Congressional Budget Office reports have estimated that the conflict depleted as much as two-thirds of U.S. missile-defense interceptors since June 2025, largely because of efforts to defend Israel against Iranian attacks. This could leave the U.S. with constrained inventories for several years.
Kagan said the deployment of three U.S. aircraft carriers to the Middle East had reduced the U.S. naval presence available in Asia, potentially giving China more room to act assertively in the region.
"I think Trump's only interest right now is in cutting economic deals with China. I don't think he has any real interest in confronting China, but that is going to lead China to be even more aggressive," he said.
In December, Trump approved an $11 billion arms package for Taiwan, but later held back on a second package worth about $14 billion, calling it a "bargaining chip" in talks with China.
China claims self-governing Taiwan as its territory. While Washington does not have a mutual defense treaty with the island, U.S. law requires it to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself.
Former CIA Director William Burns said in 2023 that Chinese President Xi Jinping had instructed the military to be ready to invade Taiwan by 2027, while stressing that this did not mean Xi had decided to launch an invasion that year or at all.
Kagan's comments come as U.S., China and Russia discuss a possible trilateral summit between Trump, Xi and President Vladimir Putin at the APEC Leaders' meeting in Shenzhen later this month.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Wednesday that Beijing was "in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state," although no agenda has been announced.
Putin had reportedly floated the idea of a three-way summit with Trump and Xi in October to discuss ending the war in Ukraine, without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the table.
"If it's clear that Donald Trump is on his way out, and the United States may be returning to something like normal, I don't want to overstate that, but they may feel both of them, both Russia and China, may feel that the time to move is in the next two years," Kagan said.

articles.title_zh: China's import expo draws more Fortune Global 500 companies, industry leaders
articles.content_orig:
This photo taken on Nov. 4, 2026 shows a view of the Hall 3 of the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai, east China. (Xinhua/Guo Lei)
SHANGHAI, Nov. 4 (Xinhua) -- The numbers of overseas companies and industry heavyweights attending the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) are both set to reach record highs, underscoring the enduring appeal of the world's largest import-themed trade fair.
The event is scheduled to open on Thursday in Shanghai, east China, with more than 300 Fortune Global 500 companies and industry leaders expected to participate, marking a record high. Additionally, more than 2,000 companies will be exhibiting here for the first time, according to organizers.
This year's expo is expected to attract a record 4,142 overseas exhibitors from 148 countries and regions. In total, 162 countries, regions and international organizations will participate, according to the Ministry of Commerce.
Since its launch in 2018, the trade fair has maintained strong appeal for international companies of all sizes, which have used the platform as a launchpad for new products in China and a fast track to enter the world's second-largest consumer market.
Danish pharmaceutical giant Novo Nordisk, which has participated in all the previous eight editions of the expo, will showcase new medicines during this year's event, including Kyinsu, a once-weekly injection for type 2 diabetes.
"The CIIE has become an important part of our work in China," said Mike Doustdar, president and CEO of Novo Nordisk. "This is our ninth consecutive year taking part, and many medicines we first presented at the expo have since launched here."
This year, over 480 exhibits are set to make their global, Asian or China debuts -- another record for the event.
Canada-headquartered athletic apparel brand lululemon will participate in the trade fair for the third consecutive year, with China now serving as its second-largest market globally.
"The CIIE is far more than a platform to showcase products," said San Yan Ng, regional president of lululemon China and APAC. "It also gives us the opportunity to engage in deeper dialogue and build stronger connections with Chinese guests, partners, government stakeholders and friends from all sectors."
The CIIE is a prominent example of China's efforts to open its market wider and facilitate entry of quality products from around the world. China expects the expanded imports will boost domestic demands and support its industrial upgrading.
The nation's imports reached 16.7 trillion yuan (about 2.48 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first nine months of this year, up 22.3 percent, the fastest growth since 2021.

articles.title_orig: UK found to be ‘dangerously’ reliant on China for critical minerals needed for defence and AI
articles.title_zh: UK found to be ‘dangerously’ reliant on China for critical minerals needed for defence and AI
articles.content_orig:
Delivering net zero also at risk, say MPs as they call for centralised policy and funding for mines and diversification
The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found.
MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme.
“Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy,” said the committee’s chair, Liam Byrne. “We cannot rearm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on.
“Yet 16 years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths, Britain remains dangerously exposed.”
It is the second time in a week that the government’s policy on China has been criticised by Byrne’s committee.
China has a stranglehold on the world’s supply of rare earths and other critical minerals, as well as their refined byproducts that are used in everything from military jets to car-locking systems and consumer products such as fridges and washing machines.
The committee heard that “the processing stage” was where the bottlenecks were, with China dominating the refining of seven categories of minerals, including refined lithium needed for electric vehicles and rare earths used in the fuselage and wings of military aircraft to help withstand temperature extremes.
MPs were told that demand for lithium alone would increase 45-fold between now and 2030, leaving the UK in a high-risk dependency relationship with China.
The demand for rare earths needed for permanent magnets used in military jets and other applications would rise 16-fold in the same period as Britain was seeking to rebuild its military capabilities.
But with China capable of suddenly turning off rare earth supplies, as it did in 2025 , a dependency on Beijing was a strategic vulnerability for the UK economy and national security, the committee found.
Separate restrictions on legacy chips after a row over a Dutch intervention in the China-owned Nexperia left the European car industry “days away” from stoppages last October.
The EU, the US and other countries faced the same risk of supplies of rare earths being cut off by China, and the committee said the UK was not putting enough effort into finding alternative supplies.
Donald Trump secured a one-year reprieve on global export restrictions on rare earths from Xi Jinping in October last year. This was extended to January 2027 after the Chinese president’s recent visit to Washington.
However, the reprieve means the UK is at the mercy of US-China relations, the report suggests.
after newsletter promotion
The most “realistic” solution was for the UK to work closely with G7 partners, the rest of Europe and Indo-Pacific countries, to “aggregate demand” and bring in new suppliers.
The committee said its investigation was frustrated by lack of transparency by the government.
“Parliament has no visibility of the capabilities the government is seeking to protect, the vulnerabilities it has identified, or the projects it is backing to reduce risk,” it said.
The committee has drawn up a 10-point plan that includes: working to identify domestic mining; refining and recycling opportunities and their costs; a strategy to encourage business to reduce procurement from China; a plan to unlock investment; and assess planning and permitting processes that may prove a barrier to mining.
As it stood, the committee said it could not be confident the government could satisfy any of its 10 tests.
“The UK requires new institutional and financial muscle,” it concluded.
A government spokesperson denied it did not have a critical minerals strategy saying it was delivering £400m “to ramp up domestic production and recycling” and forge new international partnerships. “Our strategy also sets clear goals for 2035, including meeting 10% of demand through domestic production and 20% through recycling, with no more than 60% of any critical minerals coming from any single country,” they added.
